extracted.intended_audience: Washington Post journalists, editors, stringers, and newsroom staff
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial and ethical standards used by The Washington Post newsroom covering conflicts of interest, sourcing and attribution, verification and fact-checking, corrections, taste, opinion labeling, and diversity expectations for reporting and publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: This news organization is pledged to avoid conflicts of interest or the appearance of conflict of interest wherever and whenever possible. We have adopted stringent policies on these issues, conscious that they may be more restrictive than is customary in the world of private business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key rules include: 'We pay our own way.' 'We accept no gifts from news sources.' 'We accept no free trips.' No payment (honoraria or expenses) from governments, government-funded organizations, groups of government officials, political groups or organizations that take positions on controversial issues, or any person, company or organization that a reporter/editor covers. Avoid accepting money from individuals or organizations that lobby government or try to influence issues the newspaper covers. Exceptions to the no-gift rule are few and obvious (occasional meals); free admissions to events not free to the public are prohibited except for seats not sold to the public (press boxes) or critic review tickets. Avoid entanglement with subjects of coverage. Avoid active involvement in partisan causes, community affairs, demonstrations; disclose household/business ties that could appear to compromise integrity; disclose relatives' employment or involvement that might appear compromising to department heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and editors of The Post are committed to fairness. 'Fairness results from a few simple practices' including completeness, relevance, honesty, and diligently seeking comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No story is fair if it omits facts of major importance (completeness). No story is fair if it includes essentially irrelevant information at the expense of significant facts (relevance). No story is fair if it consciously or unconsciously misleads the reader (honesty). Fairness includes giving individuals/organizations the opportunity to address assertions or claims made about them and taking that comment genuinely into account (diligent seeking of comment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste and decency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Washington Post respects taste and decency and will avoid prurience. Profanities and obscenities should be avoided unless their use is so essential to a story of significance that its meaning is lost without them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscenities may not be used without approval of executive or managing editors. If potentially offensive material has legitimate news value, editors should use visual and/or text warnings about such material (e.g., warning before linking to graphic images). The Post does not link to sites that aid or abet illegal activity; consult Legal Department when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion separation and labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The separation of news columns from the editorial pages is solemn and complete; analysis, perspective, opinion and review have distinct labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions provided: Analysis = interpretation of the news based on evidence; Perspective = discussion with a point of view, including first-person narratives; Opinion = columns or blogs in the Opinions section; Review = a professional critic’s assessment. News may include in-depth reporting, analysis or commentary when plainly labeled as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalist role and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should make every effort to remain in the audience, to be the stagehand rather than the star, to report the news, not to make the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In gathering news, journalists must not misrepresent their identity or occupation and must not portray themselves as police officers, physicians or anything other than journalists. Private behavior as well as professional behavior must not bring discredit to the profession or The Post. Clarify ground rules with sources and start interviews with presumption of on-the-record unless explicitly agreed otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and fact-checking responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Washington Post reporters have primary responsibility for reporting, writing and fact-checking their stories. Stories are subject to review by one or more editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Post has a multilevel review structure: assignment editors, multiplatform/copy editors, and senior editors. The number of editors and the extent of their involvement varies depending on complexity, sensitivity, and time pressure. Editors overseeing digital platforms may also control presentation, headlines, news alerts and newsletters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections, clarifications, and editor's notes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Washington Post strives for nimble, accurate and complete news reports and to be promptly responsive in correcting errors in digital platforms and in print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing a correction, explain clearly and quickly what was wrong and what is correct. Use a correction, clarification or editor’s note whenever substantively correcting material. Clarifications rewrite language that is factually correct but unclear or add missed context such as a newly obtained comment. An editor’s note is required when a correction calls into question the entire substance of an article or raises a significant ethical matter; a senior editor must approve an editor's note. Time stamps alone signal developing stories; do not add update notes unless there is reason to note the change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other corrections practices (alerts, social, comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections extend to alerts, social networks and comment streams; the newsroom should correct mistakes across platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an incorrect alert was sent, send a corrective alert with accurate information. When erroneous information is published on social networks, correct it on that platform. When an error is found by a reader and posted to comments, the audience engagement team should indicate in comments that it has been corrected. The Post does not attribute blame to individual reporters or editors in corrections, though may note production problems or that incorrect information came from a trusted source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take-down (unpublish) requests
rubrics_metrics.description: As a matter of editorial policy, we do not grant take-down requests, which should be vetted at the highest level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject claims inaccuracy, investigate and, if necessary, publish a correction rather than removing the article. Consider whether further editorial action is warranted (updates, follow-ups), but do not remove content as if it had never been published. Exceptions: review takedown requests when published personal data puts a person under threat of physical harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on sources and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Washington Post is committed to disclosing to its readers the sources of the information in its stories to the maximum possible extent. Transparency is honest and fair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to make reporting as transparent as possible so readers can know how and where information was obtained. Prefer named sources to unnamed sources. Describe to readers why unnamed sources deserve confidence (e.g., 'sources familiar with the thinking of defense lawyers').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of confidential (unnamed) sources
rubrics_metrics.description: When using unnamed sources, be reluctant to grant anonymity and be certain the benefit to readers is worth the cost in credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must know the identity of unnamed sources so they can assess appropriateness. Prefer at least two independent sources for factual information that depends on confidential informants; prefer sources with firsthand knowledge; relevant documents can sometimes serve as a second source. Publish from a single source only after deliberations involving executive/ managing editors and department head, based on the source’s reliability and the basis for information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: We must be truthful about the source of our information. Attribution of material from other media must be total. Plagiarism is not permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should be able to distinguish between what the reporter saw and what was obtained from other sources (wire, email, websites). The Post places a premium on original reporting. If a reporter was not present at a scene, the story should make that clear; reconstructed statements must be transparently attributed. If unsure about application, discuss with editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground rules for attribution (on the record/background/deep background/off the record)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: On the record = attributable by name; On background / not for attribution = attributable to a descriptive source; Deep background = information can be used but not attributed; Off the record = information cannot be used for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain these definitions to sources before beginning. Avoid deep background if possible because it provides no way to help readers understand origin. Be careful with off-the-record material; if someone intends 'not for attribution' when saying 'off the record,' clarify. If a source truly insists on off-the-record, generally avoid listening to information that would become unusable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with sources: fairness, context, and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat sources fairly: put statements into context, summarize arguments accurately, quote potentially controversial statements in a complete sentence or paragraph when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give people who are the subject of a story a reasonable opportunity to respond (avoid calling at the last minute when possible). Avoid blind quotations whose sole purpose is color. Do not publish ad hominem quotations from unnamed sources. Do not promise sources you will refrain from additional reporting or verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quoting sources and sharing drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective in quoting is to capture words and intended meaning accurately; do not allow sources to change rules governing quotations after the fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a source asks to read back quotations, do not allow them to change the original; permit adding to a quotation and explain sequence to readers if necessary. Sharing sections of stories with sources for technical accuracy is acceptable; sharing entire drafts is against policy except with extremely rare permission of executive or managing editors. Be prepared that communications with sources can become public; make no promises or concessions incompatible with Post standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert sources and diversity of voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive to get a rich variety of voices and avoid dependence on the same academics or public figures for reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively seek new specialists, including women, younger people, people of color, unconventional thinkers and people not routinely quoted. Also seek a broad range of individuals affected by events (e.g., students, teachers, employees) and include voices of ordinary citizens regularly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit and bylines for stringers and contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: Any significant reporting by a stringer, staff member or other Post employee should be credited in a byline or a tagline at the end of a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When such contributors take notes from broadcasts, conduct basic research or check routine facts, they need not be credited; significant reporting should be credited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of on-the-record interviews for inexperienced sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Start virtually all interviews with the presumption that they are on the record. Inexperienced sources should clearly understand they are speaking to a reporter and may be quoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish ground rules at the beginning of conversations; in taped interviews, it's preferable that ground-rule discussions are on tape. If ground rules specify attribution terms other than 'on the record,' clarify before beginning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital updating and use of timestamps
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital pieces evolve; timestamps signal developing stories and readers expect sharpening and improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is unnecessary to put notes on stories stating that a story has been updated unless there is a particular reason to note the addition of new information or other change; use corrections/clarifications/editor's notes when correcting significant mistakes or when necessary to explain editorial judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: No linking to illegal-activity content
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post does not link to sites that aid or abet illegal activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult with the Legal Department if there is a question about whether a site falls under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity policy for reporting and staffing
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity is at the core of Washington Post journalism: engage a variety of voices as interviewees and first-person writers, strive for a staff that reflects a range of backgrounds and life experiences, and seek feedback from all who would give it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Post releases an annual report on staff diversity. Make an effort to expand the universe of sources and include voices representing the readership and general population.
